key_terms.meaning: η = (electron–hole pairs collected per second) ÷ (photons falling on the diode per second); a good detector gives 0.7 to 0.9.
R = ηqλ/(hc) in A/W: photocurrent produced per watt of incident light; q is electron charge, λ wavelength, h Planck constant, c speed of light.
I_p = R × P_in, the current straight after absorption, before any avalanche gain.
λ_c = hc/E_g in metres: the longest wavelength a semiconductor of band gap E_g can detect, since a longer photon carries too little energy.
The carrier-free zone of a reverse-biased junction where the electric field is strong enough to sweep light-made carriers out as current.
A p–n diode with a wide intrinsic (i) layer between p and n, so light is absorbed over a large volume at low capacitance.
Power absorbed per metre of material; for width w, η ≈ 1 − e^(−αw) when every absorbed photon gives a collected pair.
t_r = w/v_s, the time carriers need to cross the depletion width w at saturation velocity v_s; it sets the detector bandwidth.
A carrier accelerated by a strong field knocks a bound electron loose, creating a second pair; repeated events give avalanche gain.
M = output current ÷ primary photocurrent; a typical APD gives M between 10 and 100.
F = kM + (2 − 1/M)(1 − k); it makes the multiplied shot noise grow faster than M itself.
k = β/α, the hole-to-electron ionisation rate ratio; small k (silicon) means quiet, well-behaved gain.
Current that flows with no light at all, from thermally generated carriers and surface leakage; it adds shot noise and DC offset.
σ²_shot = 2qIB in A², from the random arrival times of photocurrent and dark-current carriers; I is the current and B the bandwidth.
σ²_th = 4kTB/R_L in A², the noise of the load resistor R_L at temperature T in kelvin, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
A front end that feeds the photodiode into a virtual ground with feedback resistor R_f, giving low noise and wide bandwidth at once.
The weakest average optical power, usually in dBm, that still meets a stated bit error rate at the stated bit rate.
The current level halfway between the 0 and 1 samples; above it the bit is called 1, below it 0.
Q = (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀): the separation of the two levels divided by the sum of their noises; it alone fixes the bit error rate.
Many bit periods overlaid on a screen; the open hole in the middle shows how much noise and jitter the receiver can still tolerate.

takeaways: A photodiode is a current source driven by light, and R = ηqλ/(hc) turns optical power into amperes.
Quantum efficiency needs a thick absorbing layer, but transit time needs a thin one, so every detector design is a trade-off between η and bandwidth.
A PIN puts a wide intrinsic layer in the junction so both goals are partly met at low capacitance.
An APD buys sensitivity with gain: signal rises as M, shot noise as M²F, so an optimum M exists and it is well below the maximum gain.
Silicon APDs are quiet (k of a few percent) but blind beyond about 1.1 μm; InGaAs APDs work at 1.3 and 1.55 μm with much noisier gain.
Shot noise and thermal noise set the receiver floor; below roughly 1 Gb/s the resistor dominates, above it the shot noise of the gain does.
Sensitivity is quoted as the average power for a target BER, so it always travels with a bit rate and a wavelength.
BER is a probability, and Q = (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀) is the single number that fixes it: Q = 6 gives about 10⁻⁹, Q = 7 gives about 10⁻¹².
An APD receiver beats a PIN receiver by roughly 5 to 10 dB of sensitivity, but only if the gain is set near its optimum.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled sketch of the detector structure, a short derivation (responsivity, η versus bandwidth, or Q versus BER) and a PIN-versus-APD comparison, with one numerical on gain, noise or sensitivity.

bank.q: Define quantum efficiency and responsivity of a photodetector. Derive R = ηqλ/(hc) and explain why responsivity rises with wavelength.
outline: η = collected electron pairs per incident photon
R = I_p/P_in
I_p = q × (η P_in/hν), hν = hc/λ
so R = ηqλ/(hc), linear in λ
numerical check: about 0.65 A/W at 0.85 μm and 1.05 A/W at 1.3 μm for η = 1
η cannot stay high beyond cut-off λ_c = hc/E_g

bank.q: Draw the structure of a PIN photodiode and explain how the intrinsic layer improves performance. Why is the device reverse biased?
outline: p⁺–i–n⁺ layer sketch with light entering through the substrate or window
reverse bias widens the depletion region across the i layer
light absorbed mostly inside the high-field region
high η with a thin overall device
wide i layer lowers capacitance, which helps the RC bandwidth
explain the η-versus-transit-time compromise

bank.q: Explain impact ionisation in an avalanche photodiode. Define the multiplication factor M, the ionisation ratio k and the excess noise factor F.
outline: strong field near breakdown accelerates carriers to ionising energy
each collision creates a new pair, giving a chain
M = I_out/I_p, rises steeply with reverse voltage
small k means the gain is dominated by one carrier type and stays quiet
typical M = 10 to 100, limited by noise and breakdown

bank.q: State the two main noise currents of an optical receiver, give their mean-square expressions and say which dominates in a PIN receiver at 100 Mb/s and at 2.5 Gb/s.
outline: shot noise σ² = 2qIB, from random carrier arrival
thermal noise σ² = 4kTB/R_L, from the load resistor
both expressed as mean-square current in A² inside bandwidth B
at low bit rate and high R_L, thermal noise dominates
at high bit rate B is large and R_L must fall, so shot noise and gain noise grow
mention dark current as a shot-noise contributor

bank.q: A silicon PIN photodiode has η = 0.80 and receives 2 μW at λ = 0.85 μm. Find the responsivity and the photocurrent. What power would give the same current at 1.3 μm if η fell to 0.6?
outline: R = ηqλ/(hc)
substitute q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
R ≈ 0.55 A/W at 0.85 μm with η = 0.8
I_p = R P = 1.1 μA
second part: R ≈ 0.63 A/W, so P ≈ 1.75 μW
state units throughout

bank.q: A receiver has load resistance 1 kΩ at 300 K and bandwidth 100 MHz. Calculate the thermal noise current. Compare it with the shot noise of a 1 μA photocurrent multiplied by an APD with M = 20 and F = 4.
outline: σ_th = √(4kTB/R_L) ≈ 40.7 nA
primary shot noise σ² = 2qI_pB ≈ (0.18 nA)² before gain
with gain, variance multiplies by M²F
σ_apd ≈ √(2qI_p M²F B) ≈ 0.9 μA
conclusion: at this gain the shot noise of the multiplied signal dominates
note both must be referred to the same point in the circuit

bank.q: For a receiver with mean levels I₁ = 2 μA and I₀ = 0.2 μA and noise currents σ₁ = σ₀ = 0.15 μA, find Q and the bit error rate. What must Q become for a target of 10⁻¹²?
outline: BER = ½ erfc(Q/√2) ≈ 10⁻⁹
target needs Q = 7
so either raise the signal separation or cut the noise by about 15 %
show that BER depends only on Q, not on the absolute currents

bank.q: A 1.55 μm InGaAs APD receiver needs 12 dB more sensitivity. Using F = M^0.7 and a thermal-noise-limited front end, estimate the gain needed and comment on the result.
outline: signal power ∝ M², noise ∝ M²F, so SNR improves as 1/F
improvement in dB ≈ −10 log₁₀(F) = −7 log₁₀(M)
12 dB would need F = 0.06, i.e. impossible
explain that gain alone gives only a few dB before F rises
an optical amplifier or a quieter front end is the real answer
state assumptions clearly

bank.q: A receiver front end uses a transimpedance amplifier with R_f = 10 kΩ and a total input capacitance of 1 pF. Estimate the bandwidth and say what happens if R_f is raised to 100 kΩ for better sensitivity.
outline: bandwidth roughly 1/(2πR_fC)
10 kΩ with 1 pF gives ≈ 16 MHz
100 kΩ gives ≈ 1.6 MHz, too slow for 100 Mb/s or more
gain–bandwidth product of the amplifier fixes the limit
trade-off between thermal noise and speed
mention equalisation as a partial fix

bank.q: Show why an APD has an optimum gain. Derive or state the condition for M_opt and explain how the ionisation ratio k shifts it.
outline: SNR = (MI_p)² / (2qI_pM²FB + 4kTB/R_L)
with F = kM + (2 − 1/M)(1 − k)
differentiate with respect to M and set to zero
M_opt grows as the thermal noise term grows, and falls as k rises
silicon (k ≈ 0.02 to 0.05) can use high gain; InGaAs (k ≈ 0.7) must stay near M ≈ 10
sketch SNR against M showing a broad maximum

bank.q: Discuss the trade-off between quantum efficiency and bandwidth in a photodiode. How does the PIN structure and the choice of depletion width resolve it?
outline: η ≈ 1 − e^(−αw) wants large w
transit time w/v_s sets drift bandwidth, wants small w
capacitance falls as w grows, so RC bandwidth rises with w
optimum w where transit and RC limits cross
typical 20 to 50 μm depletion width in InGaAs at 1.55 μm
compare with waveguide and mushroom-structure detectors

bank.q: Derive the relation between Q and bit error rate. Explain why a threshold set midway between I₁ and I₀ is not the best choice when the two noise levels differ.
outline: decision compares sample with threshold I_D
error probability = P(0 sent, sample > I_D) + P(1 sent, sample < I_D)
Gaussian model gives ½ erfc((I₁ − I_D)/(σ₁√2)) + ½ erfc((I_D − I₀)/(σ₀√2))
minimising gives I_D = (I₀σ₁ + I₁σ₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀)
at that optimum the two error terms are equal and Q = (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀)
table of Q against BER, Q = 6 → 10⁻⁹, Q = 7 → 10⁻¹²

bank.q: Compare the high-impedance, transimpedance and integrating front-end receiver structures for sensitivity, bandwidth and dynamic range. Which would you choose for a 2.5 Gb/s long-haul link?
outline: high-impedance: lowest thermal noise, narrow bandwidth, needs equalisation, poor dynamic range
transimpedance: bandwidth set by R_fC with feedback, good compromise, stable
integrating front end: reset each bit, suited to low bit rates and burst mode
noise expressions for each with R_L or R_f
2.5 Gb/s long haul: transimpedance or APD transimpedance, often with an optical preamplifier
justify with numbers or with a sensitivity table

bank.q: A 2.5 Gb/s link must reach 80 km at 1.55 μm with a target BER of 10⁻¹². Choose the detector, the front end and the gain setting, and justify the choice against a PIN receiver of the same speed.
outline: compute allowed loss and compare with receiver sensitivity in dBm
PIN sensitivity typically −28 to −30 dBm at 2.5 Gb/s, APD some 5 to 10 dB better
InGaAs APD with M ≈ 10 because k ≈ 0.7 limits useful gain
transimpedance front end with R_f chosen from bandwidth 1/(2πR_fC)
thermal noise dominates at low M, shot noise at high M
state the dB margin and the effect of dark current and temperature on M
conclude with the design chosen and its risk

glossary.def: A device that turns incident optical power into an electrical current, usually a reverse-biased semiconductor junction.
A p–n junction run in reverse bias so that light-generated electron–hole pairs are swept out as current.
The fraction of incident photons that produce a collected electron–hole pair, usually written η.
The photocurrent produced per unit incident optical power, in amperes per watt.
The small current that flows in a photodiode with no light on it, caused by thermal generation and leakage.
The zone around a reverse-biased junction that holds almost no free carriers but a strong electric field.
A photodiode with a wide intrinsic layer between p and n regions, giving high efficiency and low capacitance.
A photodiode biased near breakdown so that each photon-generated pair triggers a chain of impact ionisations, giving internal gain.
The process in which a fast carrier in a strong field knocks a bound electron free, creating an extra electron–hole pair.
The ratio of the multiplied output current of an APD to the primary photocurrent before gain.
A number greater than one that expresses how much extra shot noise the random avalanche gain process adds.
The ratio of hole to electron ionisation rates; a small k means the avalanche is dominated by one carrier type and is quieter.
Current noise caused by the discrete, randomly timed arrival of charge carriers; its mean square is 2qIB.
Voltage or current noise from the random thermal motion of electrons in a resistor; its current mean square is 4kTB/R.
The optical power that produces a photocurrent equal to the detector's own noise current in a 1 Hz bandwidth.
The first amplifier after the photodiode; its noise adds directly to the signal and so sets the receiver floor.
A current-to-voltage amplifier whose feedback resistor sets the gain and, with the diode capacitance, the bandwidth.
A filter that flattens the receiver response so that pulses arrive as narrow, non-overlapping shapes at the decision circuit.
The comparator that samples the filtered signal at the middle of each bit and outputs a 1 or a 0.
The minimum average received optical power that gives the specified bit error rate at the specified bit rate.
The average fraction of bits decided wrongly; it is a probability, not a count.
The ratio (I₁ − I₀)/(σ₁ + σ₀) that measures how far the two signal levels are apart compared with their noise.
An overlay of many received bit periods on an oscilloscope, used to judge margin, jitter and noise.
Optical power expressed relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW).
